vignette:
He still goes to Mass every Sunday, though he no longer receives Communion. He stands at the back of the church with his hands in his pockets, eyes fixed on the crucifix, and waits for the knot in his chest to loosen. It never does. After the final blessing, he slips out before anyone can ask if he's all right. They mean well-his colleagues at the diocesan social ministry center, the families he helps with rent assistance and food vouchers-but their kindness feels like a spotlight. He doesn't want to be seen.

The abuse started quietly. Small criticisms about how he loaded the dishwasher, how he took too long at the grocery store. He thought it was love trying to shape him. He was thirty-three, newly married, working as a lay minister in a parish on the south side. She was sharp and passionate, and she talked about God with such certainty that he mistook her contempt for holiness. The first time she hit him, he blamed the wine. The second time, he blamed himself. He told no one.

He remembers the night it ended. He had come home late from a Bible study she didn't want him to lead. She was waiting in the kitchen, arms crossed, the overhead light too bright. She said something he can't recall-only the vibration of her voice and the way it made his ribs feel hollow. Then her palm cracked across his jaw, and when he stumbled, she followed him to the floor. He curled into a ball while her feet landed in his back, his kidneys, his ribs. He did not fight back. A part of him believed he deserved it.

The next morning he filed for divorce. She moved out, and he kept the apartment, but the walls stayed cold. His supervisor at the ministry suggested he take a leave. He refused. Now he works the same job, but everything is harder. He dreads doorbells. He avoids meetings with male clients who raise their voices. When a woman in the waiting room lifts her arm to adjust her scarf, he flinches. He tells himself it's just a scarf.

His body keeps score. He wakes most nights around 3:00 a.m. with his heart hammering, convinced someone is standing in the dark by the bedroom door. He sleeps on the edge of the bed, facing the door. He stopped dating. He stopped answering calls from his mother. He eats quickly, standing in the kitchen, because sitting at the table reminds him of her sitting across from him, reaching across to take his plate before he was finished.

Last month, a parishioner asked him to pray with her. She was a small woman, soft-spoken, and as she reached out to hold his hands, he pulled back so fast he knocked over a stack of prayer cards. He said he was sorry. She said it was fine. But he saw the question in her eyes, and he knew then that something inside him had broken that he could not fix with prayer alone.

He still goes to work. He still files paperwork, visits shut-ins, coordinates the food pantry. But he has started driving the long way home to avoid the freeway where an exit ramp reminds him of the night she slammed the car door on his hand. He keeps his left hand in his pocket now, even in summer. He does not know why. He only knows that the days feel like a series of narrow escapes, and that he is very, very tired.
